Now I solve the problem.

## Solution

**Setup.** Let $C_1$ be a vertical contour $\operatorname{Re} z = c$ (with $c > \alpha$) oriented upward, chosen so that all singularities of $\phi$ lie strictly to its left. The function $\phi(z)$ is meromorphic to the left of $C_1$ with finitely many poles $z_1, \dots, z_N$, and $\phi(z) \to 0$ as $z \to \infty$ in the half-plane $\operatorname{Re} z \le \alpha$.

**Step 1: Evaluate $f(t)$ by closing the contour to the left.**

For $t > 0$, close $C_1$ by a semicircular arc $\Gamma_R$ of radius $R$ in the left half-plane, forming a closed contour $C_R = C_1^{(R)} \cup \Gamma_R$ enclosing all poles (for $R$ large enough). On $\Gamma_R$ we have $\operatorname{Re} z \le c$, and for the portion with $\operatorname{Re} z \le \alpha$, the hypothesis gives $\phi(z) \to 0$.

By **Jordan's lemma**: for $t > 0$, since $|e^{zt}| = e^{t \operatorname{Re} z}$ decays on the left arc and $\phi(z) \to 0$ uniformly as $|z| \to \infty$ on $\Gamma_R$,

$$\int_{\Gamma_R} e^{zt}\,\phi(z)\,dz \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \quad \text{as } R \to \infty.$$

By the **residue theorem**:

$$f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{C_1} e^{zt}\phi(z)\,dz = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \operatorname{Res}\!\big[e^{zt}\,\phi(z),\; z_k\big].$$

**Step 2: Form of each residue term.**

Let $z_k = \sigma_k + i\tau_k$ be a pole of order $n_k$. Then:

$$\operatorname{Res}\!\big[e^{zt}\,\phi(z),\; z_k\big] = e^{z_k t}\,Q_k(t),$$

where $Q_k(t)$ is a polynomial in $t$ of degree $n_k - 1$ (with $Q_k$ constant when $n_k = 1$). Therefore:

$$\boxed{f(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} e^{\sigma_k t}\,e^{i\tau_k t}\,Q_k(t).}$$

**Step 3: Asymptotic behavior as $t \to \infty$.**

Set $\sigma^* = \max_k \sigma_k = \max_k \operatorname{Re} z_k$. The terms with $\operatorname{Re} z_k = \sigma^*$ dominate; all others are exponentially smaller.

**Case 1: All poles strictly to the left of the imaginary axis** ($\sigma_k < 0$ for all $k$, i.e., $\sigma^* < 0$).

Every term $e^{\sigma_k t} Q_k(t) \to 0$ exponentially (exponential decay dominates polynomial growth). Therefore:

$$\lim_{t\to\infty} f(t) = 0.$$

**Case 2: Poles on the imaginary axis, none to the right** ($\sigma^* = 0$), **and all poles on the imaginary axis are simple** ($n_k = 1$ whenever $\sigma_k = 0$).

The dominant terms are $\sum_{\sigma_k = 0} A_k\, e^{i\tau_k t}$ (constants $A_k$ since the poles are simple), and all terms with $\sigma_k < 0$ vanish. Thus:

$$f(t) \to \sum_{\sigma_k = 0} A_k\, e^{i\tau_k t} \quad \text{(oscillatory, up to vanishing error).}$$

- **Sub-case 2a:** The only pole on the imaginary axis is at the origin $z = 0$ (so $\tau_k = 0$). Then $f(t) \to A_0 = \operatorname{Res}[\phi, 0]$, a **finite constant**.
- **Sub-case 2b:** There are simple poles on the imaginary axis at $z = i\tau_k$ with some $\tau_k \neq 0$. The sum $\sum A_k e^{i\tau_k t}$ oscillates and **does not converge**; $f(t)$ has no limit (though it remains bounded).

**Case 3: A multiple pole lies on the imaginary axis** ($\sigma^* = 0$ and some $z_k$ with $\operatorname{Re} z_k = 0$ has order $n_k \ge 2$).

The corresponding term $e^{i\tau_k t}\, Q_k(t)$ has $|Q_k(t)| \sim |a|\, t^{n_k - 1} \to \infty$. Therefore $|f(t)| \to \infty$.

**Case 4: At least one pole to the right of the imaginary axis** ($\sigma^* > 0$).

The dominant term(s) grow as $e^{\sigma^* t}\, Q_k(t)$, which tends to infinity exponentially. Therefore $|f(t)| \to \infty$.

**Summary.**

$$\lim_{t\to\infty} f(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if all poles satisfy } \operatorname{Re} z_k < 0,\\[4pt] \operatorname{Res}[\phi,\, 0] & \text{if the only pole on } \operatorname{Re} z = 0 \text{ is a simple pole at } 0,\\[4pt] \text{does not exist (bounded oscillation)} & \text{if simple poles on } \operatorname{Re} z = 0 \text{ at nonzero points, none to the right},\\[4pt] +\infty \text{ in magnitude} & \text{if a multiple pole lies on } \operatorname{Re} z = 0 \text{ (none to the right)},\\[4pt] +\infty \text{ in magnitude} & \text{if some pole satisfies } \operatorname{Re} z_k > 0. \end{cases}$$

The physical interpretation: $f(t)$ is the inverse Laplace transform of $\phi$. The poles in the left half-plane correspond to decaying (transient) modes; simple poles on the imaginary axis correspond to sustained oscillations; multiple poles on the imaginary axis or poles in the right half-plane correspond to unbounded (unstable) growth. The imaginary axis is thus the **stability boundary**: $f(t) \to 0$ if and only if all poles lie strictly in the left half-plane.
